title: Whisper in the Dark
narration: A 23-watt whisper—weaker than a nightlight—is being heard from 24.9 billion kilometers away. That whisper is Voyager 1. But it won't last forever. How long until we lose it?
visual_goal: Dark starfield, a tiny blinking light in the distance, radio waves pulsing.

title: Launch of a Dream
narration: Inside that machine is a gold-plated disc holding the sound of a kiss, a baby's cry, and rain. It was sent to be found. But before it could be found, it had to survive. Launched September 5, 1977, this 722-kilogram spacecraft—Voyager 1—was built to push farther than anything we'd ever made. Its twin, Voyager 2, had lifted off 16 days earlier. But Voyager 1 took the faster path. On board: a message in a bottle, made of gold and copper.
visual_goal: Historical launch footage, liftoff, the Golden Record close-up.

title: Giants and Fire
narration: In 1979, Voyager 1 reached Jupiter. It found something no one expected—volcanoes erupting on a moon called Io. For the first time, we saw worlds that could burn. Then, in 1980, it swung past Saturn. And then it set its course away from the planets, toward the edge of the solar system—a direction no probe had ever taken. But not forever. Its power was already fading.
visual_goal: Jupiter and Io volcanic eruption, Saturn ring flyby animation.

title: Into the Beyond
narration: For nearly 35 years, Voyager 1 sailed outward. On August 25, 2012, it crossed the heliopause—the boundary where the solar wind yields to interstellar space. That put it 166 astronomical units from the Sun, over 24.9 billion kilometers away. To communicate, it sends a signal that takes 22 hours and 40 minutes to reach Earth. That's the distance light travels in one direction—if you shouted from Earth, it would take nearly a day for Voyager to hear you.
visual_goal: Animated crossing of a boundary, transition to starry interstellar space, distance graphic.

title: The Long Silence
narration: By 2030, its power source will fade, and it will fall silent. But it will keep sailing. And one day—maybe a million years from now—someone else will find it. The record holds the sounds of Earth—the murmur of a mother, the crackle of thunder, the rhythm of a heartbeat. It's a time capsule of who we were. When they find it, the first thing they'll hear is a baby's cry. What will that say about us?
visual_goal: Voyager drifting away, fading light, Earth in distance, poetic shot.
